blocks.quote: 01 The idea A first intuition: predict the next word.

Ask your phone a question. The answer appears one word at a time. Under the hood, the model is doing one thing: predicting the next token. A large language model is a program trained on text. It returns a probability for every possible next token. Pick one, append it, and run again. That is the autoregressive loop: auto because the model feeds its own output back in, regressive because each prediction is a regression on the sequence so far. How does a pile of numbers become a sentence? Follow one token through the machine.
The model in your pocket · demo 01a A search box, a voice query, an AI answer and the links below it. The animation runs once when the demo comes into view.
Takeaway The search engine does not look up a stored answer. The summary is written one token at a time, and the same loop runs in the data centre behind it.

The aha At its heart, it is a loop: one word after another. Pick a likely next word, append it to the input, and run the whole thing again. A sentence, an answer, or a program emerges from that repeated step.
Next step · code It writes text and code.
The same loop writes prose and code; Python runs the program.
From a request to a program · demo 01a · code The model writes the code; Python runs it.
sky.py
Write a Python program that calculates how strongly blue and red light are scattered in the atmosphere. Sure. The program computes the Rayleigh scattering ratio for 450 nm and 650 nm.
Terminal
Blue is 4.35× more strongly scattered than red.
Takeaway The model wrote the program; the program computed the ratio. Code is another sequence the loop can predict, one token at a time.
02 Play the loop One Word After Another

Context is everything the model can see when it predicts the next token: the text in the input field, the conversation so far, and the instructions or examples that frame the exchange. Training taught it how to read such a frame, so a prompt can bring out a role, a tone, or a way of answering. The model has no other working memory. One word after another is a slow feeling-forward in a complex world. At every step very much is possible, but not all of it makes sense; the loop is how the model narrows that space. The demo shows the idea, not a trained model. The next token is drawn from a distribution, appended, and the loop repeats. Temperature controls how far the model drifts from the most likely path. Why not always take the top token? Greedy does. Top-p keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p, then samples. Low temperature sharpens the distribution; high temperature flattens it.

The autoregressive loop · demo 01 Let the demo choose the next word, or switch between sampling, greedy, and top-p. Each choice opens only the continuations that make sense from there, so the tree narrows as you go.
live
Sampling draws from the whole distribution; temperature controls how concentrated it is.
Sample Greedy Top-p 0.9
Let it choose → Reset Temperature

Why "temperature"? In a gas, temperature sets how widely molecular speeds are spread (Maxwell-Boltzmann). Here it plays the same role for logits: . High T flattens the distribution; low T sharpens it; greedy is the limit T → 0, and exact zero is handled by taking the top token directly. The name is a metaphor: there is no gas inside the model.
Step 0 / 6 Context length 7 words Top choice dragon Choice sample
Takeaway The distribution is the model; the choice is how you draw from it. Greedy, sampling, and top-p all read the same probabilities differently.

The probability tunnel · demo 01b A single prediction is one slice through a landscape of plausible continuations. The main path is the deepest blue valley, the route the model finds most likely. Every other option sits in its own side basin, close enough to remain possible. Step through the sentence and watch the valley narrow as context closes options; turn up the temperature and watch it widen again. Drag to rotate.

Think of every point in this landscape as an embedding: a vector that stands for a word or a continuation. Neighbouring points are similar in meaning, and the depth of a valley is the probability the model gives that continuation. The blue path is only one possible route through this space. The other paths are the alternatives the model has learned to consider; they are its experience compressed into the geometry of the space. The context is the part of the landscape the model can see right now: it shifts the valleys and closes routes that no longer fit. This picture is an abstraction. A real model works in thousands of dimensions, with far more paths than can be drawn here. The energy-landscape view follows the energy-based learning framework of LeCun et al., A Tutorial on Energy-Based Learning (2006) .
context
deep blue = likely path gold = possible exits gold plane = all other tokens small dots = other plausible tokens
Next word capital
Next word → Temperature

The green ball is the current context. Each token gives it direction and momentum; it rolls into the deepest valley, the path of least resistance. The gold dashed lines are plausible exits out of the main valley. Raise the temperature and the ridges flatten, so even more of those exits become reachable. Takeaway The model never decides that something is right. It builds a distribution from its training data and draws from it; the landscape shows how context narrows that distribution.
The model does not jump to an answer. It feels its way through this space, one token at a time. Click a word below the landscape, or use Next word, to jump to that step.

Training is the process that shapes this landscape. The model moves its coarse points, the token and context representations, into relations with one another so that meaning can be stored in compressed form inside the network. Attention and dense layers are trained together. In the high-dimensional space behind the projection, the loss makes the ball move faster along paths that continue the training text and slower along paths that do not. The landscape is therefore learned, not given: what counts as plausible is defined entirely by the training data.
03 Inside the model A model is a stack of functions.

A neural network is built by applying functions one after another. One layer transforms its input, the next layer transforms that result, and the stack turns a small operation into a deep model. The depth is composition: many simple steps, each feeding the next. Classical programming starts with the procedure: you write down every step, and the computer executes it. AI reverses that: you provide enough examples with matching outputs, and training searches for the function in between. The layers are the shape that function takes; the data decides what it does.
The transformer: six steps, one running vector.

The stack of functions above is the transformer. For every token, it runs the same six steps, again and again. The model moves points in a high-dimensional space. Training shapes those points so that the final context vector has smaller angles to words that plausibly come next than to words that do not. Because the decision is about angles, not straight-line distances, this page uses the great-circle metric by default. The model works on a hypersphere of directions; to draw it, we project that sphere down to three dimensions. Plausible here means the continuation occurred in the training data; it does not mean that the model has a separate notion of truth. For every token, again and again, it asks how that token stands in context to all the other tokens right now. Attention lets it look around, a dense layer and an activation function transform each token, and LayerNorm keeps the numbers in a stable range. A few other parts do their jobs along the way. Each pass shifts the token's point in the space. The directions follow meaning paths and become clearer, so the last token ends up at a small angle to the tokens that are likely next in this context. That is the trick.
Now we explain these building blocks step by step: tokenize, embed, add position, attend, feed-forward, and the residual stream. The order is the real architecture; the demos are simplified.
Step 1 · Tokenize Tokenize: text becomes a sequence of IDs

A token is not a word. Text is encoded as numbers: every character has a code point, and a byte-level tokenizer starts from 256 bytes, so every string is representable. Rare words split into subwords: “unbelievable” becomes “un”, “believ”, “able”, and the same “un” appears in “unhappy” and “unmarried”. A space can be a token too.
understanding unbreakable The transformer is playing greatly
A real tokenizer learns its merge table from text. IDs are addresses into an embedding table.
Step 2 · Embed Embed: IDs become points in meaning space Meaning becomes geometry

Each token ID points to a learned vector. A real model uses thousands of dimensions; the demo uses two so you can see it. Similar words sit close, and a direction can carry a relationship: man → woman is the same arrow as king → queen. The axes here are labelled for humans; a real model's axes are unlabelled. Sometimes the relation does not come out exactly; an approximate direction is already enough to be useful.

From one axis to two · demo One axis orders words by temperature. Pick two words and see where their midpoint lands; the embedding demo below adds a second direction, so the same words can carry more relations.
1D: temperature
In the same space, word vectors add and subtract. Treat each word as an arrow from the origin: add two arrows and the result lands near the word that combines their meanings.
Embedding arithmetic · demo Pick an example. The vectors add and subtract in the same two-dimensional space, and the result lands near a word.
King − Man + Woman Man + 2 · Power Prince + Power male ↔ female power all directions
The space has two learned directions in this demo. Choose an example to see where it lands.
From relations to translation

The points form a manifold: locally flat, globally curved. The relations are similar enough to translate: the path from one word to another can be transformed into the corresponding path in another language. Feed-forward networks learn such transformations. This is an approximation. In a real model the geometry is much messier: relations overlap, exceptions are common, and translation is learned from huge amounts of text rather than read off a clean map. The intuition still points in the right direction.
Loading the manifolds …
Step 3 · Positional embedding Position: every slot gets its own fingerprint

Attention has no sense of order. Without a position signal, “man bites dog” and “dog bites man” are the same bag of vectors. A sinusoidal encoding adds a fingerprint to every slot: each pair of dimensions oscillates at a different frequency.
Context length
Visible dimensions
Each position gets a fingerprint built from slow and fast waves.
Each row is one position; each column is one dimension.

Same pattern, one dimension higher From the flat slice to the 3D curve The curve is a small, readable slice of that geometry. A real model is far more complex, but it follows the same geometric principles in thousands of dimensions. In the first three dimensions the curve is a spiral: the first two dimensions turn in a circle, while the third drifts slowly. The Euclidean view measures the straight-line chord from the token to the current point on that spiral. Switch to the angle view and the same points are projected onto the unit sphere, and in a real model onto a hypersphere: the distance is now the great-circle arc, the angle between the token direction and the position direction. The spiral stays, but the question changes from how far apart the two points are to how far their directions have turned. position × dimension → 3D curve → N dimensions
Position
Euclidean length Angle to the word
Auto-rotate view

The three axes are the first three dimensions; the blue sphere is the word, the arrow its position. Drag to rotate. A real model adds the position vector to the token embedding and compares the resulting context vectors; the demo keeps the two vectors separate so the angle stays visible. A real model uses thousands of dimensions.
Step 4 · Attend Self-attention: context pulls the word into place

How does a word know which neighbours matter? Self-attention lets each token look at the others, decide which matter, and pull their information into its vector. That is how “bank” moves toward the river or money reading. A real layer has many heads; the demo shows one.
no unambiguous context river in context money in context both in context

This is an intuition, not a real head. A real head computes query, key, and value vectors, turns their dot products into weights with a softmax, and sums the value vectors. Each head has one unit of attention. If it puts 80% on one word, only 20% remains for the others. Many heads can attend to different things.
The layer in detail · the MLP FFN: a projection, a bias, a bend

After attention, each token passes through its own small network, the MLP. It projects the vector, applies a nonlinearity, and projects back. The bend is what lets a straight cut separate what was inseparable.
Dense unit
FFN
Worked example · 2 inputs, 2 outputs
Each output is a dot product plus a bias, then the activation. The matrix above shows the arithmetic.
Depth without a nonlinearity
two dense layers without a nonlinearity
Without a nonlinearity, two layers collapse into one. Depth adds no expressive power.
Nonlinear activation functions
A nonlinearity is applied to each coordinate after the projection. ReLU folds at zero; sigmoid and tanh bend smoothly; GELU is smooth but not monotonic.
ReLU flat, then a rise
GELU smooth, small dip
Sigmoid S-shape, 0 to 1
tanh S-shape, -1 to 1
Where the bend happens After attention, the MLP moves the token toward a region where the next token is easier to separate.

Watch the MLP bend the space · demo 07 A straight line is the easiest separator, but it is not always possible in the original space. The MLP lifts the points into a new plane where it becomes possible. In an LLM the same idea runs in thousands of dimensions and helps the model isolate and represent internal states.
← Back Next → ⟲
Takeaway The layers in an MLP lift the points into a higher-dimensional space where a straight line can separate what was inseparable before. They change the space in which the cut is made.

Real models do this in thousands of dimensions. Separation and translation are two views of the same learned transformation. Visual idea after C. Keup & M. Helias, Origami in N dimensions ( arXiv:2203.11355 ).
Step 5 · Feed-forward FFN: a pattern matches, a value is written
The feed-forward network works on each token separately. It expands the vector, applies an activation, and projects back. Attention mixes tokens; the FFN computes within a token.
I ate the apple I bought an Apple laptop
Residual stream “Apple” + context
Patterns in W₁
Next-token pull in W₂
Written back richer or more specific vector
What is simplified: a real FFN has no labelled keys or values. The patterns are learned directions in W₁; the pull is a learned direction in W₂.

One layer is a small function A simple layer does not need to be complicated. It multiplies its input by a learned matrix W, adds a learned vector b, and passes the result through an activation function. The activation adds a bend, a nonlinearity. Without it, any number of dense units would collapse into one linear map. A simple layer can look like this: one matrix, one bias, one activation. That is a dense unit. It is the basic building block; a transformer layer later combines self-attention and an FFN. Real networks combine building blocks differently. A convolutional layer is built for images, an attention layer for sequences, a dense layer for tables of numbers. A transformer layer is not one dense unit: it combines self-attention, which mixes information between tokens, with an FFN, which is itself a small stack of dense units. They share the same idea: functions with parameters, trained on data so that their output gets closer to the right answer.
04 The stack One layer, then the stack.
01 Tokenizer context → tokens → 02 Embedding tokens → vectors → 03 Layers × N Self-attention + FFN → 04 Unembedding vector → scores

01 Tokenizer. The context is split into tokens, and each token gets an ID. The tokenize demo shows the step. 02 Embedding. Each ID points to a learned vector. The embedding demo shows how meaning becomes geometry. 03 Layers × N. One layer is self-attention plus an FFN: attention mixes tokens, the FFN rewrites each vector. The same shape runs N times, each layer with its own weights. The attention demo shows one head; the composition below shows the whole layer. 04 Unembedding. The last vector becomes scores over the vocabulary, and softmax turns them into a distribution. The last step shows the move from vector to word.

Why scores become probabilities Softmax turns arbitrary scores into something that behaves like a probability distribution. It exponentiates every score, so all values become positive, then divides by the sum. The exponential is monotone, so the largest score stays the largest; the division makes the results sum to one. Shifting every score by the same constant cancels in the ratio, so the absolute range of the scores does not matter. The base is a convention: any positive base gives a valid distribution, but with the derivative stays clean and the training signal well behaved. The name “softmax” comes from Bridle (1990) .
Self-attention
Softmax

W, b, W1, and W2 are parameters; training adjusts them. activation() is a nonlinearity such as ReLU or GELU. Self-attention takes the whole matrix X (one row per token) and returns A with one row per token. The weights α_ij lie in [0,1] and sum to 1 for each i. The FFN then transforms each row A_i separately; it never receives the whole matrix. Softmax turns the final scores into a distribution over the vocabulary; it preserves their ranking. This is a coarse picture. Underneath, every step is a matrix of numbers; the formulas show the shape of the computation, not the implementation.

The layer is the whole composition A layer is not just attention and not just an FFN. It is the composition: attention mixes the tokens into A, then the FFN rewrites each row of A. The result is the next matrix X with the same shape. In a real block, residual connections and normalization wrap both steps; the formula keeps the shape visible.

A language model combines these and other building blocks A language model combines these building blocks into a transformer block: self-attention first asks how strongly each word is connected to every other word in the context, and the model learns those connections from data. An FFN then untangles the result: it folds the vectors into a higher-dimensional space, separates features, and folds them back. A real transformer layer also contains layer normalization, residual connections, and other pieces. They are left out here so the picture stays readable; the residual section at the end of this chapter covers them in detail. At the start, a matrix X goes in: one row per token, each row a vector. At the end, a matrix of the same shape comes out, but the values have changed. The last token has absorbed the meaning of the whole context. The unembedding turns its vector into scores for every vocabulary token; those scores point to a region of token directions with small angles, and softmax draws one. How the context is mixed Inside a layer, self-attention looks at the whole context. For every token, it scores how much that token should take from every other visible token. The scores form a token-by-token matrix: one row for the token asking, one column for the token answering. The self-attention demo below shows one head doing this.
Causal self-attention
Token The capital of France The 100% — — — capital 80% 20% — — of 10% 30% 60% — France 5% 45% 10% 40%
row = token asking column = token answering masked = future token
The mix
Token 2 reads token 1 and itself. It cannot read token 3, because token 3 comes later. The upper triangle is masked.

Each head looks from a different perspective Attention does not choose its weights from a fixed list. It learns, from the loss, which aspects of the visible tokens help predict the next token. With enough data, memorizing every training sentence is not an option, so the model is pushed toward reusable structure: gender, age, syntactic role, topic, or whatever else lowers the loss. Each head can look at the same tokens from a different perspective: one head can track a pronoun, another a verb, another the topic, and each can ignore what the others use.
Head 1 pronoun “it” → “bank” Head 2 verb “sat” → “bank” Head 3 topic “river” → “bank”
A sketch, not measured weights: the heads see the same tokens, but each can attend to something else.

“To think is to forget a difference, to generalize, to abstract. In the overly replete world of Funes there were nothing but details, almost contiguous details.” <cite>Jorge Luis Borges, “Funes the Memorious” (1942) · Spanish original </cite>

Borges's Funes remembers everything and therefore cannot think. To think, he has to forget differences, generalize, and abstract; the story's point is not that memory is bad, but that thinking needs a cut. An LLM does the same at two scales. The model as a whole does not store every fact; it learns compressed regularities. A single head does not need to represent everything at once; it can focus on one aspect and ignore the rest. The stack then recombines the cuts into a rich context. The first layer mixes the original token vectors. Later layers mix vectors that earlier layers have already changed, so every pass sees a different context. In an autoregressive model the matrix is lower-triangular: a token can attend to itself and earlier tokens, never to tokens that come later. That causal mask is what lets the model train on every prefix of a sentence and predict the next token without seeing the future. After attention, each token's new vector goes through a feed-forward network. The FFN works on one token at a time: it separates features and rewrites the vector. Attention moves information between tokens; the FFN transforms what each token carries. The FFN section opens that step. Local meaning, then wider context Early layers can learn local patterns. One layer may notice that “new” and “york” belong together; a later layer can use that combined meaning as a new unit and mix it with a wider context. A single layer can solve a small task, or several layers can solve one together. Deep models work by composing these small transformations. The stack repeats. Each layer has its own learned weights, so the structure is shared but the parameters are not. After the last layer, the unembedding reads the last token's vector and produces a distribution over the next token. The real GPT-2 trajectories below show the movement through 12 of these blocks; the last step turns the final vector into a word.
Step 6 · Residual Residual stream: every layer adds to the same stream

Every layer reads the same running vector, computes an update, and adds it back. Think of a shared notebook: earlier notes stay, later layers read them and add more. The new state is the old state plus a change.
The new state is the old state plus what the layer adds. The demos are simplified; the order is the real architecture.
The cat sat on the mat because she was tired . Embedding every word becomes a vector. Attention “she” points back to “cat”. MLP “tired” explains why the cat sat.
One shared page. Each layer writes in its own color, and earlier notes stay readable.
running stream
Nothing is overwritten, so the original signal survives and gradients have a short path back. That is why deep networks train.
05 The block repeats The whole block: attention + FFN, again and again

Attention and the FFN are one transformer block. The same architecture runs again and again, but each layer has its own learned weights and its own learned vectors. The block repeats in structure, not in parameters. Each pass lets every token look at the context, then moves it through its own MLP. Below, real GPT-2 trajectories show the same movement. Each line is one token, each bend is one block. The vectors live in 768 dimensions, too many to picture, so the plot projects them down to three. What you see is not the real motion but its PCA shadow. The angular view is the default because the model compares directions, and “plausible” means the continuation is frequent in its training data, not that it is true.

Token trajectories through GPT-2 · real PCA Real hidden states from GPT-2 small for “The capital of France is”. Each line follows one token through the embedding and 12 blocks. Each state has 768 dimensions, too many to picture, so this is not the real motion: PCA keeps the three directions where the states change most and flattens everything onto them. The 3D points are a shadow. Lines that cross here need not touch in the full space, and a flat-looking bend can hide a large move.

Euclidean distance measures the straight-line gap, like a tape measure. The model compares directions: in the angular view every vector is normalized to the unit sphere, where the angle is the metric that matters. The real model does this in 768 dimensions; the 3D sphere is its PCA shadow.

Real GPT-2 small hidden states, normalized per layer and PCA-reduced to 3D. Drag the slider to move through the layers. The next-token candidates appear at the final layer; the highlighted one is the model's top choice.
06 The last step The final vector picks a word.

The last token carries the whole context in its final vector . A learned unembedding matrix turns it into one score per vocabulary token. has one row per token. The dot product is the logit ; the vector collects all logits. After normalization, that dot product is the cosine of the angle between and ; the great-circle view shows that angle. In GPT-2 is often tied to the input embedding matrix, but it is still a learned matrix.

Softmax turns the logits into probabilities: , where sums over the whole vocabulary. Why not simply divide each logit by the sum? Logits can be negative or zero, so the result would not be a probability. The exponential makes every value positive and preserves the order; dividing by the sum gives numbers between 0 and 1 that add to 1. It also turns differences into ratios: adding the same constant to every logit changes nothing. The largest score gets the most mass, but the alternatives keep some.

Geometrically, points to a region of token directions. Each token owns a region; near a seam two words are almost equally likely. More tokens shrink the cells, but the seams never close. Mabrok (2026) calls the band around a seam the expressibility gap.
The map of words · demo 08 Every word owns a cell. Move the pointer; the thought falls into the nearest cell. The golden seams are where two words are equally near.
Nearest word Dog Wins with — Margin to seam — Ambiguous share —
Move the pointer across the map.

Takeaway Words divide the space of thoughts into cells. Certainty is being deep inside a cell; uncertainty is standing on a seam or right at the edge. The model can think more finely than one word can say. More words make smaller cells and thinner seams, but the ambiguous share never reaches zero. In a real model the space has thousands of dimensions and the vocabulary has tens of thousands of tokens.

From logits to a probability distribution · demo 09 Real GPT-2 small scores for two prompts. The left side is the raw logit from each dot product; the right side is what softmax makes of it. Switch the context and watch the whole distribution change.
real GPT-2
spaceship deserted planet
context “As the spaceship was approaching the ”
token logit
probability softmax
Hovered token — Logit — exp((logit − max) / T) — Probability —
Hover a token. The ribbon shows how its score becomes probability. The temperature slider changes only the softmax, not the logits.

Takeaway Softmax does not create the ranking; the dot products do. It turns scores into a distribution that sums to one, and temperature decides how sharply the winner is favoured. Real GPT-2 small logits for “As the spaceship was approaching the”, from the Transformer Explainer (Polo Club, Georgia Tech). The absolute logit offset is arbitrary; softmax depends only on differences.
07 The whole loop Text in, geometry, one word out.

The pieces fit in a fixed order: text → tokens → vectors → position → attention + residual → FFN → distribution → draw → append . The loop ends when the model emits the special token <|endoftext|> . No step has a tidy fact database. Knowledge is distributed across the weights, and meaning lives in the geometry. A pile of numbers becomes a sentence one token at a time.

What it is A next-token predictor: one distribution, one draw, one append, repeated. Why it works More context and more layers narrow the distribution, so the next token becomes easier to choose. Its limits It predicts plausible text. It can be fluent and wrong, and it offers no guarantee of truth. The fixed order text → tokens → vectors → position → attention + residual → FFN → distribution → draw → append . The loop ends when the model emits <|endoftext|> .

Think of every point in this landscape as an embedding: a vector that stands for a word or a continuation.
Neighbouring points are similar in meaning, and the depth of a valley is the probability the model gives that continuation.

The other paths are the alternatives the model has learned to consider; they are its experience compressed into the geometry of the space.
The context is the part of the landscape the model can see right now: it shifts the valleys and closes routes that no longer fit.
This picture is an abstraction.
A real model works in thousands of dimensions, with far more paths than can be drawn here.

It builds a distribution from its training data and draws from it; the landscape shows how context narrows that distribution.
The model does not jump to an answer.
It feels its way through this space, one token at a time.

Training is the process that shapes this landscape.
The model moves its coarse points, the token and context representations, into relations with one another so that meaning can be stored in compressed form inside the network.
Attention and dense layers are trained together.
In the high-dimensional space behind the projection, the loss makes the ball move faster along paths that continue the training text and slower along paths that do not.
The landscape is therefore learned, not given: what counts as plausible is defined entirely by the training data.
03 Inside the model A model is a stack of functions.
A neural network is built by applying functions one after another.
One layer transforms its input, the next layer transforms that result, and the stack turns a small operation into a deep model.
The depth is composition: many simple steps, each feeding the next.
Classical programming starts with the procedure: you write down every step, and the computer executes it.
AI reverses that: you provide enough examples with matching outputs, and training searches for the function in between.
The layers are the shape that function takes; the data decides what it does.
The transformer: six steps, one running vector.
The stack of functions above is the transformer.
For every token, it runs the same six steps, again and again.
The model moves points in a high-dimensional space.
Training shapes those points so that the final context vector has smaller angles to words that plausibly come next than to words that do not.
Because the decision is about angles, not straight-line distances, this page uses the great-circle metric by default.
The model works on a hypersphere of directions; to draw it, we project that sphere down to three dimensions.
Plausible here means the continuation occurred in the training data; it does not mean that the model has a separate notion of truth.
For every token, again and again, it asks how that token stands in context to all the other tokens right now.
Attention lets it look around, a dense layer and an activation function transform each token, and LayerNorm keeps the numbers in a stable range.
A few other parts do their jobs along the way.
Each pass shifts the token's point in the space.
The directions follow meaning paths and become clearer, so the last token ends up at a small angle to the tokens that are likely next in this context.
Now we explain these building blocks step by step: tokenize, embed, add position, attend, feed-forward, and the residual stream.
The order is the real architecture; the demos are simplified.
Step 1 · Tokenize Tokenize: text becomes a sequence of IDs
Text is encoded as numbers: every character has a code point, and a byte-level tokenizer starts from 256 bytes, so every string is representable.
Rare words split into subwords: “unbelievable” becomes “un”, “believ”, “able”, and the same “un” appears in “unhappy” and “unmarried”.
A space can be a token too.

Step 3 · Positional embedding Position: every slot gets its own fingerprint
Attention has no sense of order.
Without a position signal, “man bites dog” and “dog bites man” are the same bag of vectors.
A sinusoidal encoding adds a fingerprint to every slot: each pair of dimensions oscillates at a different frequency.
Each position gets a fingerprint built from slow and fast waves.
Each row is one position; each column is one dimension.
Same pattern, one dimension higher From the flat slice to the 3D curve The curve is a small, readable slice of that geometry.
A real model is far more complex, but it follows the same geometric principles in thousands of dimensions.
In the first three dimensions the curve is a spiral: the first two dimensions turn in a circle, while the third drifts slowly.
The Euclidean view measures the straight-line chord from the token to the current point on that spiral.

Switch to the angle view and the same points are projected onto the unit sphere, and in a real model onto a hypersphere: the distance is now the great-circle arc, the angle between the token direction and the position direction.
The spiral stays, but the question changes from how far apart the two points are to how far their directions have turned.

Step 4 · Attend Self-attention: context pulls the word into place
How does a word know which neighbours matter?
Self-attention lets each token look at the others, decide which matter, and pull their information into its vector.
That is how “bank” moves toward the river or money reading.
A real layer has many heads; the demo shows one.
no unambiguous context river in context money in context both in context
This is an intuition, not a real head.
A real head computes query, key, and value vectors, turns their dot products into weights with a softmax, and sums the value vectors.
Each head has one unit of attention.
If it puts 80% on one word, only 20% remains for the others.
Many heads can attend to different things.

After attention, each token passes through its own small network, the MLP.
It projects the vector, applies a nonlinearity, and projects back.

Step 5 · Feed-forward FFN: a pattern matches, a value is written
The feed-forward network works on each token separately.
It expands the vector, applies an activation, and projects back.
Attention mixes tokens; the FFN computes within a token.
I ate the apple I bought an Apple laptop
Residual stream “Apple” + context
Written back richer or more specific vector
What is simplified: a real FFN has no labelled keys or values.
The patterns are learned directions in W₁; the pull is a learned direction in W₂.
One layer is a small function A simple layer does not need to be complicated.
It multiplies its input by a learned matrix W, adds a learned vector b, and passes the result through an activation function.
The activation adds a bend, a nonlinearity.
Without it, any number of dense units would collapse into one linear map.
A simple layer can look like this: one matrix, one bias, one activation.
It is the basic building block; a transformer layer later combines self-attention and an FFN.
Real networks combine building blocks differently.
A convolutional layer is built for images, an attention layer for sequences, a dense layer for tables of numbers.
A transformer layer is not one dense unit: it combines self-attention, which mixes information between tokens, with an FFN, which is itself a small stack of dense units.
They share the same idea: functions with parameters, trained on data so that their output gets closer to the right answer.

Why scores become probabilities Softmax turns arbitrary scores into something that behaves like a probability distribution.
It exponentiates every score, so all values become positive, then divides by the sum.
The exponential is monotone, so the largest score stays the largest; the division makes the results sum to one.
Shifting every score by the same constant cancels in the ratio, so the absolute range of the scores does not matter.
The base is a convention: any positive base gives a valid distribution, but with the derivative stays clean and the training signal well behaved.
The name “softmax” comes from Bridle (1990) .
W, b, W1, and W2 are parameters; training adjusts them.
activation() is a nonlinearity such as ReLU or GELU.
Self-attention takes the whole matrix X (one row per token) and returns A with one row per token.
The weights α_ij lie in [0,1] and sum to 1 for each i.
The FFN then transforms each row A_i separately; it never receives the whole matrix.
Softmax turns the final scores into a distribution over the vocabulary; it preserves their ranking.
This is a coarse picture.
Underneath, every step is a matrix of numbers; the formulas show the shape of the computation, not the implementation.
The layer is the whole composition A layer is not just attention and not just an FFN.
It is the composition: attention mixes the tokens into A, then the FFN rewrites each row of A.
The result is the next matrix X with the same shape.
In a real block, residual connections and normalization wrap both steps; the formula keeps the shape visible.

A language model combines these and other building blocks A language model combines these building blocks into a transformer block: self-attention first asks how strongly each word is connected to every other word in the context, and the model learns those connections from data.
An FFN then untangles the result: it folds the vectors into a higher-dimensional space, separates features, and folds them back.
A real transformer layer also contains layer normalization, residual connections, and other pieces.
They are left out here so the picture stays readable; the residual section at the end of this chapter covers them in detail.
At the start, a matrix X goes in: one row per token, each row a vector.
At the end, a matrix of the same shape comes out, but the values have changed.
The last token has absorbed the meaning of the whole context.
The unembedding turns its vector into scores for every vocabulary token; those scores point to a region of token directions with small angles, and softmax draws one.
How the context is mixed Inside a layer, self-attention looks at the whole context.
For every token, it scores how much that token should take from every other visible token.
The scores form a token-by-token matrix: one row for the token asking, one column for the token answering.

Each head looks from a different perspective Attention does not choose its weights from a fixed list.
It learns, from the loss, which aspects of the visible tokens help predict the next token.
With enough data, memorizing every training sentence is not an option, so the model is pushed toward reusable structure: gender, age, syntactic role, topic, or whatever else lowers the loss.
Each head can look at the same tokens from a different perspective: one head can track a pronoun, another a verb, another the topic, and each can ignore what the others use.
Head 1 pronoun “it” → “bank” Head 2 verb “sat” → “bank” Head 3 topic “river” → “bank”
A sketch, not measured weights: the heads see the same tokens, but each can attend to something else.
“To think is to forget a difference, to generalize, to abstract.
In the overly replete world of Funes there were nothing but details, almost contiguous details.” <cite>Jorge Luis Borges, “Funes the Memorious” (1942) · Spanish original </cite>
Borges's Funes remembers everything and therefore cannot think.
To think, he has to forget differences, generalize, and abstract; the story's point is not that memory is bad, but that thinking needs a cut.
An LLM does the same at two scales.
The model as a whole does not store every fact; it learns compressed regularities.
A single head does not need to represent everything at once; it can focus on one aspect and ignore the rest.
The stack then recombines the cuts into a rich context.
The first layer mixes the original token vectors.
Later layers mix vectors that earlier layers have already changed, so every pass sees a different context.
In an autoregressive model the matrix is lower-triangular: a token can attend to itself and earlier tokens, never to tokens that come later.
That causal mask is what lets the model train on every prefix of a sentence and predict the next token without seeing the future.
After attention, each token's new vector goes through a feed-forward network.
The FFN works on one token at a time: it separates features and rewrites the vector.
Attention moves information between tokens; the FFN transforms what each token carries.
The FFN section opens that step.
Local meaning, then wider context Early layers can learn local patterns.
One layer may notice that “new” and “york” belong together; a later layer can use that combined meaning as a new unit and mix it with a wider context.
A single layer can solve a small task, or several layers can solve one together.
Deep models work by composing these small transformations.
Each layer has its own learned weights, so the structure is shared but the parameters are not.
After the last layer, the unembedding reads the last token's vector and produces a distribution over the next token.

Step 6 · Residual Residual stream: every layer adds to the same stream
Every layer reads the same running vector, computes an update, and adds it back.
Think of a shared notebook: earlier notes stay, later layers read them and add more.
The new state is the old state plus a change.
The new state is the old state plus what the layer adds.

06 The last step The final vector picks a word.
The last token carries the whole context in its final vector .
A learned unembedding matrix turns it into one score per vocabulary token.
The dot product is the logit ; the vector collects all logits.
After normalization, that dot product is the cosine of the angle between and ; the great-circle view shows that angle.
In GPT-2 is often tied to the input embedding matrix, but it is still a learned matrix.
Softmax turns the logits into probabilities: , where sums over the whole vocabulary.
Why not simply divide each logit by the sum?
Logits can be negative or zero, so the result would not be a probability.
The exponential makes every value positive and preserves the order; dividing by the sum gives numbers between 0 and 1 that add to 1.
It also turns differences into ratios: adding the same constant to every logit changes nothing.
The largest score gets the most mass, but the alternatives keep some.
Geometrically, points to a region of token directions.
Each token owns a region; near a seam two words are almost equally likely.
More tokens shrink the cells, but the seams never close.
Mabrok (2026) calls the band around a seam the expressibility gap.

07 The whole loop Text in, geometry, one word out.
The pieces fit in a fixed order: text → tokens → vectors → position → attention + residual → FFN → distribution → draw → append .
The loop ends when the model emits the special token <|endoftext|> .
No step has a tidy fact database.
Knowledge is distributed across the weights, and meaning lives in the geometry.
A pile of numbers becomes a sentence one token at a time.
What it is A next-token predictor: one distribution, one draw, one append, repeated.
Why it works More context and more layers narrow the distribution, so the next token becomes easier to choose.
Its limits It predicts plausible text.
It can be fluent and wrong, and it offers no guarantee of truth.
